title: Prime Video Home
seoTitle: Design the Prime Video (Streaming Service) Home Page
description: Design the personalised home page of a video streaming service like Prime Video or Netflix — rows of titles chosen per user, candidate generation and ranking, entitlements, artwork, and serving millions of page loads quickly.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is the Prime Video Home Page?
blocks.text: When you open a streaming app, the home page shows rows like "Continue watching", "Top 10 in your country" and "Because you watched…", each filled with title artwork. Every user sees a different page, it must load almost instantly on TVs, phones and browsers, and it can only include titles the user is entitled to watch in their country.

items: Users should see a personalised home page: an ordered list of rows, each with an ordered list of titles.
Rows include personal ones (continue watching, watchlist, recommendations) and editorial or trending ones.
Only titles available in the user's region and entitled by their subscription should appear (with clear labels for rent/buy or add-on channels).
Users can scroll rows horizontally and the page vertically, loading more on demand.

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: The first screen renders in < 1 second, including on living-room devices.
Highly available: if personalisation fails, show a sensible non-personalised page rather than an error.
Scale to ~200M users with a big evening peak (~100k page loads per second).
"Continue watching" reflects what the user just watched within a minute.
Perfect freshness of recommendations (hours old is fine).
**Title**: movie or series, metadata, artwork variants, availability windows per region.
**Row**: type (personal, editorial, genre), title and a list of title IDs.
**Page**: ordered rows for a user on a device.
**Entitlement**: what a user can watch (subscription, channels, rentals).

blocks.code:
GET /home?device=tv&cursor= -> { rows: [{ id, title, items: [{ titleId, artUrl, badge }] }], nextCursor }
GET /rows/:rowId?cursor=        -> more items for a row

blocks.text: Row content comes from several sources: **offline recommendation jobs** precompute "Because you watched" and "Top picks" per user each day; **editorial** rows are curated; **trending** rows are computed per region every few minutes; **continue watching** and **watchlist** come from live user stores.

The **Home Service** gathers candidate rows for the user, filters items by **region and entitlements**, removes duplicates across rows, and ranks the rows themselves (a user who binges documentaries gets that row higher). It then **hydrates** each title with metadata and the right artwork for the device.

Only the first few rows and the first ~10 items per row are returned. More rows arrive as the user scrolls down, and more items as they scroll right, using cursors. This keeps the first response small and fast.
1) How do we load the page in under a second?

approach.text: Run recommendation models and query every source when the user opens the app.

challenges.text: Model inference and many sequential calls blow the latency budget at 100k requests per second.

approach.text: Precompute heavy personal rows offline and store them in a key-value store by user. At request time, fetch all row sources **in parallel** with strict timeouts.

challenges.text: Still hydrating hundreds of titles per request.

approach.text: Precompute personal rows, and cache **shared rows** (trending, editorial, genre) per region and entitlement segment, since millions of users see the same ones. Title metadata and artwork URLs are cached in memory in the Home Service. Each source has a **timeout and fallback**: if recommendations are slow, substitute a popular-in-region row. Artwork images come from a CDN, sized per device.

challenges.text: Cached shared rows must still be filtered per user's exact entitlements, which must be fast (a bitmap or set check).

blocks.text: 2) How do we keep "Continue watching" fresh?

The player sends progress events every few seconds; a stream processor updates the user's **viewing progress** store and removes finished titles (or advances to the next episode). The Home Service always reads this row live, while the rest of the page may come from caches. When the user returns from watching, the app re-requests just that row.
Mention device differences: a TV home page shows fewer, larger tiles and has more memory constraints than mobile, so the API takes the device type and returns layout-appropriate rows and artwork.
3) How do we personalise row order and artwork?

Beyond choosing rows, a ranking model orders rows by predicted engagement for the user, with diversity constraints (not five comedy rows in a row). Artwork can be **personalised too**: each title has several artwork variants and a bandit picks the one most likely to appeal to this user. All of this is logged to measure impact with A/B tests.

quiz.question: Why precompute personal recommendation rows?
options: Running models on every page load is too slow and expensive
quiz.explanation: Offline jobs store rows per user for fast lookup.

quiz.question: What should happen if the recommendation source times out?
options: Fall back to a popular-in-region row

quiz.question: Which rows can be cached and shared across users?
options: Trending and editorial rows per region and segment
quiz.explanation: Millions of users see the same shared rows.

quiz.question: Why load only the first few rows initially?
options: To keep the first response small so the screen renders fast
quiz.explanation: Lazy loading fetches more as the user scrolls.
